title: Graph Alignment via Dual-Pass Spectral Encoding and Latent Space Communication
claim: Embedding-based unsupervised alignment breaks down under feature noise, structural noise, and training variation, even when the underlying graphs are essentially the same.
layout: 4 panels in a row, scatter plots, left-to-right, lettered captions below
description: Four side-by-side 2D scatter plots show node embeddings of two graphs, G1 as blue filled circles and G2 as orange crosses. Each panel has a legend in the bottom right. Panel (a), Identical Graphs, shows the orange crosses sitting exactly on the blue circles, so the embeddings match perfectly. Panel (b), Feature Inconsistency, shows the orange crosses scattered around the blue points with visible offsets. Panel (c), Structure Inconsistency, shows a stronger mismatch. The orange points are more spread out and there are a few outliers. Panel (d), Different Trainings, shows the largest divergence. The orange cloud is shifted and stretched in a different direction from the blue points. The eye goes first to the clean overlap in (a), then follows the growing separation of blue and orange across (b) to (d). Captions are in a serif font under each panel.
caption: Limitations of embedding-based graph alignment on synthetic data. $\mathcal{G}_1$ is a ring graph with 100 nodes and 2D random features. (a) $\mathcal{G}_2$ is identical to $\mathcal{G}_1$, yielding well-aligned embeddings. (b) Feature inconsistency introduced through Gaussian noise (std=0.2) causes divergence. (c) Structural inconsistency via 30% edge dropout distorts the embedding alignment. (d) Identical graphs with different training runs show embedding instability, highlighting unsupervised learning limitations.
abstract: Graph alignment, the problem of identifying corresponding nodes across multiple graphs, is fundamental to numerous applications. Most existing unsupervised methods embed node features into latent representations to enable cross-graph comparison without ground-truth correspondences. However, these methods suffer from two critical limitations: the degradation of node distinctiveness due to oversmoothing in GNN-based embeddings, and the misalignment of latent spaces across graphs caused by structural noise, feature heterogeneity, and training instability, ultimately leading to unreliable node correspondences. We propose a novel framework employing a dual-pass encoder to inject high-frequency discriminability into node features, paired with a geometry-aware functional map module that learns bijective and isometric transformations to align latent spaces while acting as a low-pass filter on correspondences, enforcing smoothness and robustness as a structural prior in map space. Extensive experiments on graph benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing unsupervised alignment baselines, exhibiting superior robustness to structural inconsistencies and challenging alignment scenarios. The implementation is available at https://github.com/maysambehmanesh/GADL.
